Serving · 2026-11-13

A cache hit is not the end of the journey

Our cache hit rate was 98.6%, yet the first token still took 3.6 seconds. Following the bytes showed where the time went, and why a hit-rate dashboard can mislead.

98.6%cache hit rate, 3.6 s first token
57%of first-token time was KV transfer
35 → 2.5s first-token p50 with admission control

Split the first token into stages

We stitched together per-request logs from four layers (gateway, entry, prefill and decode) for 5,858 requests between October 19 and 21, then attributed the average first-token time to each stage.

The transfer volume did not depend on the hit rate at all. It was a straight line in input length.

Two causes. First, prefix reuse was not enabled on the decode side, so prefill always sent KV from token zero. Second, the gateway applied session affinity only to prefill (99.4% of turns returned to the same prefill node) while only 6.7% of decode turns returned to the same decode node. A third finding was about reading metrics: a "connect 1.6 s" field was really time spent waiting for prefill to finish; the handshake itself took tens of milliseconds.

Route to where the KV already is

For GLM, consistent hashing sends a session back to the same prefill node, which raised the prefix hit from 0.64 to 0.98. For GLM-5.3-Flash, routing by prefix to the same replica gives near-100% affinity. Hit rates today: GLM 97–99%, DeepSeek about 96%.

Say no when the system is full

Read a hit, don't recompute it

  • Another machine's memory over RDMA is about 7× faster than local NVMe and as fast as local memory. Across the cluster, about 39 TB of memory can act as one shared KV pool.
  • Writes to host memory must stay on the local NUMA side: split writes from 8 GPUs reach 144 GB/s; writing everything to one side drops to 46 GB/s.
  • One GPU sending to many machines does not add bandwidth. To go faster, use more GPUs and more NICs at once.
